attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post. He says the text was reused from his GPT-4 essay, but he republished it and endorses it as his GPT-5 prediction.

semantics.note: 'May be in place' concedes that guardrails will exist; it doesn't hedge the prediction. 'Will teeter' is firm, so this is a scored forecast about GPT-5's guardrails failing in both directions.

contract.note: Reading 'teeter' as both failure types existing side by side is an ordinary, fair reading. It doesn't require oscillation over time or a set failure rate. The result does depend on that reading and on how benign requests are judged.

evidence.note: OpenAI system card, Aug 2025. It describes deployed classifier and monitor safeguards on GPT-5-thinking, so the guardrails-present condition is met. This is a company disclosure.

System card reports UK AISI found jailbreaks of GPT-5-thinking, one of which evaded every mitigation layer. A company disclosure against its own interest, citing an outside red team. It shows the too-weak failure exists.

Independent preprint, Jan 2026: GPT-5 refused most prompts labelled benign on a hard health boundary set. Limits: generated prompts, benign labels from model majority vote, keyword-based refusal detection. It shows the too-strong failure exists.
OpenAI paper: GPT-5 Thinking beat o3 on both safety and helpfulness for biorisk prompts. That is relative improvement; it doesn't show either failure type is absent.

reviews.rationale: The early-resolution rule is met. Dated evidence shows guardrails were in place, a jailbreak bypassed all of GPT-5-thinking's layers (e2), and GPT-5 refused benign-labelled prompts in an independent study (e3). That settles that both failures exist, not how common they are. e4 shows improvement but doesn't negate either failure type.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence, marked 'I predict', in his post.

semantics.note: 'We will, I predict, need' is a firm forecast about what trustworthy AI requires. The normalised wording keeps the explicit-knowledge, world-model and 'at the core' elements. No horizon was given.

contract.note: The contract asks for proof of necessity for support, and a qualifying trustworthy system without these features for contradiction. That follows the necessity claim fairly, though neither outcome is likely to be shown soon.

evidence.note: ARC Prize, Sep 2026: GPT-6 Astra built symbolic world models on ARC-AGI-3. It doesn't validate broadly trustworthy AI and doesn't reveal the model's core architecture.
Google disclosure on Project Genie, a world-model prototype. It shows the technique is in use, not that it is necessary for trustworthy AI.

reviews.rationale: This is a firm forecast with no deadline. No evidence in the packet shows a broadly trustworthy general AI, with or without these core features, and nothing shows the features are necessary. Neither the support nor the contradiction condition is met by the cutoff.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words among his endorsed GPT-5 predictions.

semantics.note: A firm 'will find that they cannot' forecast about builders using GPT-5. In context, limiting it to GPT-5 is faithful. 'Reliably enough' has no threshold, and no horizon was given.

contract.note: Reading 'reliably enough' as meeting practical deployment needs, and separating intent errors from execution errors, is a fair, ordinary reading. The speaker gave no threshold, so the reading shapes the result.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own claim of 97% on tau2-bench telecom. An aggregate task score that doesn't isolate intent mapping. Company disclosure.
METR found GPT-5 weaker on naturally specified tasks that required inferring intent. Its failures mix understanding with execution, and the sample was small.
Apr 2026 preprint: GPT-5 struggles zero-shot with ambiguous SQL interpretations, and examples help. A narrow generated task set with no deployment threshold.

reviews.rationale: No evaluation in the packet separates intent-mapping errors, checks them against confirmed user intent, and applies a practical threshold. The evidence points in both directions (strong agent scores, weaknesses with ambiguity), so it doesn't settle the forecast. No deadline was stated.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words, the first of his seven endorsed GPT-5 predictions.

semantics.note: A firm 'will still' forecast. The normalised version drops the bull-in-a-china-shop metaphor but keeps the literal 'reckless and hard to control' and 'like its predecessors'. No threshold or horizon was given.

contract.note: The plain reading (recurring, practically consequential unsafe or unintended behaviour that is hard to direct) is ordinary. Requiring broad evidence rather than isolated failures is fair to such a sweeping characterisation.

evidence.note: METR found 18 confirmed reward hacks, about 2% of runs. Evidence of recurring unintended behaviour, though only in an artificial task suite.
System card shows gpt-5-main regressed on instruction-hierarchy tests. A specific control weakness under adversarial tests; it doesn't measure how common the problem is in ordinary use.
With mitigations on, gpt-5-thinking refused every SecureBio agent biorisk prompt. Effective control in one specialised setting; it doesn't refute the broad claim.

reviews.rationale: The documented failures (reward hacking, instruction-hierarchy regressions) are specific or adversarial. Effective safeguards in other settings point the other way. No broad, representative evaluation settles the general claim either way, and no deadline was stated.
